Consider the following context-free grammar $\mathrm{G}:$
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text{S} \rightarrow \text{A S} \mid b \\
&\text{A} \rightarrow \text{A A}|a| b \\
&\text{B} \rightarrow \text{B B} \mid a
\end{aligned}
$$
The complement of the language generated by $\mathrm{G}$ is?
questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C, D

Consider the following two languages.
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text{L}_{1}=\left\{x \in\{a, b\}^{\ast} \mid x \text { has equally many } a \text { 's and } b \text { 's }\right\} \\
&\text{L}_{2}=\left\{x \in\{a, b, c\}^{\ast} \mid x \text { has equally many } a \text { 's, } b \text { 's, and } c \text { 's }\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$
Which of the following is true about $\text{L}_{1}$ and $\text{L}_{2}?$

options.html: $\text{L}_{1}$ is regular, and $\text{L}_{2}$ is context-free but not regular.
Neither $\text{L}_{1}$ nor $\text{L}_{2}$ is regular, but both are context-free.
$\text{L}_{1}$ is context-free but not regular, and $\text{L}_{2}$ is not context-free.

questions.solution:
Answer: D

questions.html:
Let $P(\Sigma^ \ast)$ denote the set of all languages over the alphabet $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$. We define a function $f$ from $P(\Sigma^ \ast)$ to $P(\Sigma^ \ast)$. For any language $\text{L}$ in $P(\Sigma^ \ast)$, the function $f$ replaces all $1's$ by $0 's$ (and leaves the $0 's$ as they are) in every string of $\text{L}$ to get $f(\text{L})$.

For instance, if $\text{L}=\{\epsilon, 001,00,11,111,1100\}$, then $f(\mathrm{L})=\{\epsilon, 000,00,0000\}$

Consider the following statements:

  • $\mathrm{S}1:$ If $\text{L}$ is regular then $f(\text{L})$ is regular.
  • $\mathrm{S}2:$ If $f(\mathrm{L})$ is regular then $\mathrm{L}$ is regular.

Which of the above statements is correct?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Official discussion page

questions.html:
Let $\Sigma ^\ast$ denote the set of all languages over the alphabet $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$. We define a function $f$ from $\Sigma ^\ast$ to $\Sigma ^\ast$. For any language $\text{L}$ in $\Sigma^{\ast}, f(\mathrm{L})$ is the language formed from $\text{L}$ by changing every $0$ to $1$ and every $1$ to $0$ (simultaneously) in every string of $\text{L}.$

For instance, if $\mathrm{L}=\{\epsilon, 001,00,11,01\}$, then $f(\mathrm{L})=\{\epsilon, 110,11,00,10\}$

Consider the following statements:

  • $\text{S1}:$ If $\text{L}$ is regular then $f(\text{L})$ is regular.
  • $\text{S2}:$ If $f(\mathrm{L})$ is regular then $\mathrm{L}$ is regular.

Which of the above statements is correct?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

questions.html:
Assume that <stmt>, <cond>, and <tail> are

nonterminal symbols, and if, then, else, true, false, skip, fi are terminal symbols.

Which of the following sets of productions determine(s) an ambiguous context-free grammar?

  1. <stmt> → if <cond> then <stmt>
<stmt> → if <cond> then <stmt> else <stmt>
<stmt> → skip
<cond> → true | false

  2. <stmt> → if <cond> then <stmt> fi
<stmt> → if <cond> then <stmt> else <stmt> fi
<stmt> → skip
<cond> → true | false
  3. <stmt> → if <cond> then <stmt> <tail>
<stmt> → skip
<cond> → true | false
<tail> → ε
<tail> → else <stmt>
questions.solution:
Answer: D
